title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
hook: spring arrives in the forest, and Radha sees Krishna dancing with everyone but her

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti and the opening of the Gita Govinda: dark clouds, Radha told to take him home, and the refrain jaya jagadisha hare.

Clove vines curl in a soft southern breeze. Bees hum around the flowering trees. The cuckoo is calling. Jayadeva piles up the details of spring until the forest seems almost too sweet to stand in. Into it walks Radha, with a friend at her side, and the friend points. Look. There's Hari, playing in the spring woods, dancing with the young cowherd women. The song's refrain says this season is hard on anyone apart from the one they love. And Radha is standing at the edge of the dance, apart.
screen: `CLOVE VINES, BEES, THE CUCKOO.` → `LOOK: HARI IS DANCING.` → `RADHA, AT THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: The friend keeps singing, in paraphrase. Here, in the lovely spring, Hari plays, dancing with the young women: a cruel season for those apart from love. She describes him, one woman after another drawing close, each sure she has his attention. And Radha, the poem says, goes away. Not to confront him. She slips off into a bower of vines, hurt and jealous, and sits by herself. She doesn't stop loving him. In her song, she remembers him: the flute, the playful glances, the way he looked at her. Even while she's angry, her mind keeps returning to Hari. She tells her friend that her heart won't let him go, though he's with the others. That's the bhakti the poem cares about. Devotion, in the Gita Govinda, isn't calm. It isn't a pleasant feeling on a good day. It has jealousy in it, and hurt, and memory, and the stubborn turning of the heart back to the one it loves. Some Vaishnava traditions have a name for this longing in separation, viraha, and treat it as a doorway rather than a failure. Radha's ache at the edge of the dance becomes, for them, a picture of the soul when God seems to be everywhere except close. The poem doesn't scold her for being jealous, and doesn't hurry to fix things. It lets her sit in the bower and remember. Spring keeps blooming around her the whole time. And somewhere in the forest, as we'll hear tomorrow, Krishna has noticed she's gone.
screen: `HARI DANCES IN THE SPRING WOODS.` · `RADHA SLIPS AWAY TO A BOWER.` · `SHE KEEPS REMEMBERING HIM.` · `VIRAHA: LONGING IN SEPARATION.` · then, large: `THE HEART TURNS BACK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time you stood at the edge of something, a party, a group, apart from the one you most wanted near, and let the memory be there without arguing, like Radha in the bower. Notice what the heart does, whether it turns away or keeps turning back. If you pray, you can bring that longing, as it is, to the one you pray to; if not, let spring keep blooming around the feeling.
Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In Radha's bower, it's longing that keeps turning back, even when it hurts.
Your line: still remembering him. Tomorrow, more of the Gita Govinda. Day nine hundred seventy-six, done.

howItsDone: In Vaishnava devotion, the Gita Govinda's songs of Radha's longing are sung and danced, and viraha, longing in separation, is honored as a mood of devotion in its own right.

chat.says: Radha gets jealous and walks away. Doesn't that mean her devotion failed?
options: No, she keeps remembering him even while hurt; that turning back is the bhakti here.
Yes, real devotion is always calm, so her jealousy shows she lost it.
Yes, and the poem scolds her so readers learn never to feel that way.
chat.meaning: In the bower, Radha's mind keeps returning to Hari. Some Vaishnava traditions call this longing in separation viraha: a doorway, not a failure.

Radha.meaning: the cowherd girl Krishna loves in the Gita Govinda

Hari.meaning: a name of Vishnu and Krishna: the one who takes away

Jayadeva.meaning: the poet who wrote the Gita Govinda

viraha.meaning: longing in separation from the one you love

Vaishnava.meaning: devoted to Vishnu, or Krishna, as the supreme God

Gita Govinda.meaning: the song of Govinda: Jayadeva's love poem of Radha and Krishna
